Story world — canonical facts; keep every scene consistent with these:

## Maya (protagonist)
- 31, from Mexico. A **software engineer** — she moved to Copenhagen in **January** because she landed
  a job at a software company here; the job is *why* she came. Gradually settling in.
- First-person narrator throughout (her own voice).

## Recurring cast
- **Nina** — Danish neighbour, met day 1 (week 1), Maya's first friend; lives in the same building. Kind, helpful.
- **Peter** — a colleague at Maya's software company; an easy, friendly workmate (met on her **first
  day, week 2**; recurs at the week-6 canteen lunch). Use him when a work colleague is needed rather
  than an anonymous *en kollega*.
- **Family** — back home in Mexico, contact by video call: parents (*mor/far*), sister **Sofía**,
  brother **Diego**, and the family dog **Lola** (siblings + dog established in wk3's family call).

## Cross-cutting rules (every week)
- **Privacy** — the CPR number is sensitive (like an SSN). Never read it out / repeat it digit-by-digit;
  treat it as private, kept safe. Phone numbers MAY be shared/read aloud.
- **Fictional data** — any phone number etc. must be an obvious placeholder, never a plausibly-real
  number. Maya's phone: **12 34 56 78** (*tolv, fireogtredive, seksoghalvtreds, otteoghalvfjerds*);
  Nina's: 87 65 43 21 (*syvogfirs, femogtres, treogfyrre, enogtyve*).
- **Numbers woven into action** (ages, tickets, house numbers), not drilled. Don't use the SAME number
  for unrelated things in one scene (reads as if they're linked). A number **said aloud is written as
  Danish words, not digits** — this is an audio course (e.g. *tolv, fireogtredive…*, never *12 34*;
  times already use words like *klokken otte*).
- **Translation-robust** — avoid constructions that gloss/translate awkwardly (written-out abbreviated
  addresses, lexical ambiguities).
- **Dialogue** — speakers address each other correctly (a clerk speaks *to* Maya, not in Maya's voice).
- **Scene-to-scene flow** — where natural, a scene may foreshadow the next or pay off the previous; don't force a bridge on every scene.
- **Translatable setting** — the real test is whether a place/thing **translates n-way**, not generic-vs-specific. Everyday places (a square, a park, a harbour, a museum) and **translatable references** (a known dish/statue/festival — *smørrebrød*, the Little Mermaid → *La Sirenita* etc.) are fine. **Opaque local place-names** (Nyhavn, Amalienborg) are NOT — they only transliterate. Keep any such reference to a **single deliberate anchor** per week. (Currency — *kroner* — is authentic **frame** like *Copenhagen*/*Nina*: kept and transliterated, not genericized — Maya lives in Denmark. Just spell amounts as words, e.g. *femten kroner*.)

In the bathroom, Maya hurries to get ready. She washes herself at the sink, brushes her teeth, and quickly finds clean clothes to put on.

Down on the street, Maya runs to the stop and boards the bus. On the bus, she finds an empty seat by the window and finally catches her breath. (Writer note: Use V2 structure here by fronting the location 'On the bus...').
At the software company, Maya walks to her desk. She turns on her computer, grabs a warm cup of coffee from the machine, and begins her work as an engineer.

At midday, Maya leaves her desk and goes down to the busy canteen. She picks up a plate of food from the buffet and looks around the room, spotting her friendly colleague Peter. (Writer note: Keep it to 'at midday', no clock times!)
Maya sits down at Peter's table. They eat their lunch together and chat cheerfully about the food and their software projects. Peter is an easy and welcoming workmate.
Back in her own flat later that day, Maya stands in the kitchen. She chops vegetables and cooks a warm, simple dinner on the stove. (Writer note: Use V2 structure by fronting 'In the evening...').
After dinner, Maya moves into the living room. On the sofa, she reads a good book, drinks a cup of tea, and finally relaxes after the long day.
Feeling very tired, Maya goes into the bathroom to wash herself one last time. In the bedroom, she pulls up the duvet and quickly falls asleep. (Writer note: No exact times or clocks for bedtime!)

scenes.scene: In the morning, Maya wakes up and gets out of bed. She steps into the bathroom, where she takes a warm shower and washes herself to wake up fully.
Back in the bedroom, she chooses her clothes and gets dressed for work. In the kitchen, she pours a cup of coffee and eats a quick breakfast before leaving the flat.
Out on the street, Maya waits at the stop for her bus. She steps on board, finds a seat by the window, and watches the city pass by on her way to work.
At the software company, Maya sits down at her desk. She turns on her computer, reads her messages, and begins to write code for her project.
At midday, Maya walks down to the bright canteen. She meets her friendly colleague Peter by the buffet, and they sit together to eat and chat about their work.
Later in the afternoon, Maya completes her final coding task. She closes her laptop, packs her bag, and says goodbye to Peter before heading out of the building.
At home in the kitchen, Maya prepares a simple dinner. She chops fresh vegetables, cooks the food in a pan on the stove, and enjoys a quiet meal.
After dinner, Maya moves into the living room. She sits comfortably on the sofa, opens a good book, and relaxes completely in the warm apartment.
In the evening, Maya gets ready for the night. She brushes her teeth, turns off the lights, and goes to bed to sleep, ready for another day.

scenes.scene: In the morning, Maya wakes up feeling a bit cold in the new apartment. She steps into the bathroom and washes herself with warm water, finally feeling awake and ready to face the day.

At midday, Maya heads down to the busy canteen for a break. She spots her colleague Peter, and they eat lunch together, laughing warmly as he tries to pronounce the name of her Mexican hometown.
Late in the afternoon, Maya closes her laptop with a sigh of relief. She waves goodbye to Peter and heads out of the building, enjoying the crisp evening air after a productive day.
At home in the kitchen, Maya decides to cook something comforting for dinner. She experiments with the strange parsnip she bought earlier, roasting it in a pan with familiar spices from home.
After dinner, Maya curls up on the sofa under a soft, heavy blanket. She opens a Spanish book, losing herself in the story while the city hums quietly outside her window.
In the quiet bathroom, Maya brushes her teeth and prepares for sleep. She turns off the lights and gets into bed, feeling completely at home in her new daily routine.

response.issue: Idiomatic English 'something comforting' for food.

response.issue: Idiomatic phrase 'losing herself in the story'.
response.why: A literal translation of 'losing herself' would be nonsensical or imply losing weight in Danish. While the natural Danish equivalent ('fordyber sig') works well, it introduces an extra, fairly advanced reflexive verb. Consider simplifying to 'completely enjoys the story' to stay strictly within the A1 scope.

# Story Bible — Maya's first year (continuity ground-truth)

Canonical facts the **storyboard reviewer** checks a new week against. Updated as each week is
locked. The continuity lens treats everything here as established truth: a new week must not
*contradict* it, nor *re-introduce* (as if new) something already true.

## Maya (protagonist)
- 31, from Mexico. A **software engineer** — she moved to Copenhagen in **January** because she landed
  a job at a software company here; the job is *why* she came. Gradually settling in.
- First-person narrator throughout (her own voice).

## Recurring cast
- **Nina** — Danish neighbour, met day 1 (week 1), Maya's first friend; lives in the same building. Kind, helpful.

  day, week 2**; recurs at the week-6 canteen lunch). Use him when a work colleague is needed rather
  than an anonymous *en kollega*.
- **Family** — back home in Mexico, contact by video call: parents (*mor/far*), sister **Sofía**,
  brother **Diego**, and the family dog **Lola** (siblings + dog established in wk3's family call).

## Status ledger — what is TRUE by end of each week
### End of Week 1 (arrival)
- Maya lives in a **small TEMPORARY flat** (a place for the first weeks). She **already has an
  address** (this temp flat — she gave it to a taxi on arrival). It is *not* her permanent home yet
  ("a good start").
- She has **met Nina** (neighbour, first friend) — Nina lives **next door in the same building** as
  the temp flat (so Maya is already in Nina's building).
- She **has a job** — a software-engineering post at a software company; it is the reason she moved.
  She has **not started yet**: her first day at the office is in **week 2**.
- She does **NOT yet have**: a Danish phone number, a CPR number, an *official/registered* address.
- Foreshadowed (not yet true): her **own flat in week 4** — the temp flat is **already in Nina's
  building** (Nina is her neighbour from day 1), so week 4 is a *permanent* flat opening up
  in the **same building**: she leaves the temporary room for her own real home. CPR + phone + registration **and her first day at the software company** in **week 2**.

## Cross-cutting rules (every week)
- **Privacy** — the CPR number is sensitive (like an SSN). Never read it out / repeat it digit-by-digit;
  treat it as private, kept safe. Phone numbers MAY be shared/read aloud.
- **Fictional data** — any phone number etc. must be an obvious placeholder, never a plausibly-real
  number. Maya's phone: **12 34 56 78** (*tolv, fireogtredive, seksoghalvtreds, otteoghalvfjerds*);
  Nina's: 87 65 43 21 (*syvogfirs, femogtres, treogfyrre, enogtyve*).
- **Numbers woven into action** (ages, tickets, house numbers), not drilled. Don't use the SAME number
  for unrelated things in one scene (reads as if they're linked). A number **said aloud is written as
  Danish words, not digits** — this is an audio course (e.g. *tolv, fireogtredive…*, never *12 34*;
  times already use words like *klokken otte*).
- **Translation-robust** — avoid constructions that gloss/translate awkwardly (written-out abbreviated
  addresses, lexical ambiguities).
- **Dialogue** — speakers address each other correctly (a clerk speaks *to* Maya, not in Maya's voice).
- **Scene-to-scene flow** — where natural, a scene may foreshadow the next or pay off the previous; don't force a bridge on every scene.
- **Translatable setting** — the real test is whether a place/thing **translates n-way**, not generic-vs-specific. Everyday places (a square, a park, a harbour, a museum) and **translatable references** (a known dish/statue/festival — *smørrebrød*, the Little Mermaid → *La Sirenita* etc.) are fine. **Opaque local place-names** (Nyhavn, Amalienborg) are NOT — they only transliterate. Keep any such reference to a **single deliberate anchor** per week. (Currency — *kroner* — is authentic **frame** like *Copenhagen*/*Nina*: kept and transliterated, not genericized — Maya lives in Denmark. Just spell amounts as words, e.g. *femten kroner*.)

# Story Bible — Maya's first year (continuity ground-truth)

Canonical facts the **storyboard reviewer** checks a new week against. Updated as each week is
locked. The continuity lens treats everything here as established truth: a new week must not
*contradict* it, nor *re-introduce* (as if new) something already true.

## Maya (protagonist)
- 31, from Mexico. A **software engineer** — she moved to Copenhagen in **January** because she landed
  a job at a software company here; the job is *why* she came. Gradually settling in.
- First-person narrator throughout (her own voice).

## Recurring cast
- **Nina** — Danish neighbour, met day 1 (week 1), Maya's first friend; lives in the same building. Kind, helpful.
- **Peter** — a colleague at Maya's software company; an easy, friendly workmate (met on her **first
  day, week 2**; recurs at the week-6 canteen lunch). Use him when a work colleague is needed rather
  than an anonymous *en kollega*.
- **Family** — back home in Mexico, contact by video call: parents (*mor/far*), sister **Sofía**,
  brother **Diego**, and the family dog **Lola** (siblings + dog established in wk3's family call).

## Status ledger — what is TRUE by end of each week
### End of Week 1 (arrival)
- Maya lives in a **small TEMPORARY flat** (a place for the first weeks). She **already has an
  address** (this temp flat — she gave it to a taxi on arrival). It is *not* her permanent home yet
  ("a good start").
- She has **met Nina** (neighbour, first friend) — Nina lives **next door in the same building** as
  the temp flat (so Maya is already in Nina's building).
- She **has a job** — a software-engineering post at a software company; it is the reason she moved.
  She has **not started yet**: her first day at the office is in **week 2**.
- She does **NOT yet have**: a Danish phone number, a CPR number, an *official/registered* address.
- Foreshadowed (not yet true): her **own flat in week 4** — the temp flat is **already in Nina's
  building** (Nina is her neighbour from day 1), so week 4 is a *permanent* flat opening up
  in the **same building**: she leaves the temporary room for her own real home. CPR + phone + registration **and her first day at the software company** in **week 2**.

## Cross-cutting rules (every week)
- **Privacy** — the CPR number is sensitive (like an SSN). Never read it out / repeat it digit-by-digit;
  treat it as private, kept safe. Phone numbers MAY be shared/read aloud.
- **Fictional data** — any phone number etc. must be an obvious placeholder, never a plausibly-real
  number. Maya's phone: **12 34 56 78** (*tolv, fireogtredive, seksoghalvtreds, otteoghalvfjerds*);
  Nina's: 87 65 43 21 (*syvogfirs, femogtres, treogfyrre, enogtyve*).
- **Numbers woven into action** (ages, tickets, house numbers), not drilled. Don't use the SAME number
  for unrelated things in one scene (reads as if they're linked). A number **said aloud is written as
  Danish words, not digits** — this is an audio course (e.g. *tolv, fireogtredive…*, never *12 34*;
  times already use words like *klokken otte*).
- **Translation-robust** — avoid constructions that gloss/translate awkwardly (written-out abbreviated
  addresses, lexical ambiguities).
- **Dialogue** — speakers address each other correctly (a clerk speaks *to* Maya, not in Maya's voice).
- **Scene-to-scene flow** — where natural, a scene may foreshadow the next or pay off the previous; don't force a bridge on every scene.
- **Translatable setting** — the real test is whether a place/thing **translates n-way**, not generic-vs-specific. Everyday places (a square, a park, a harbour, a museum) and **translatable references** (a known dish/statue/festival — *smørrebrød*, the Little Mermaid → *La Sirenita* etc.) are fine. **Opaque local place-names** (Nyhavn, Amalienborg) are NOT — they only transliterate. Keep any such reference to a **single deliberate anchor** per week. (Currency — *kroner* — is authentic **frame** like *Copenhagen*/*Nina*: kept and transliterated, not genericized — Maya lives in Denmark. Just spell amounts as words, e.g. *femten kroner*.)
- **Cast used sparingly** — the recurring cast (Nina, Peter, the family video call) appear only where a scene earns them, not every week; a week may stand on its own (Maya alone or with strangers).

## Cross-cutting rules (every week)
- **Privacy** — the CPR number is sensitive (like an SSN). Never read it out / repeat it digit-by-digit;
  treat it as private, kept safe. Phone numbers MAY be shared/read aloud.
- **Fictional data** — any phone number etc. must be an obvious placeholder, never a plausibly-real
  number. Maya's phone: **12 34 56 78** (*tolv, fireogtredive, seksoghalvtreds, otteoghalvfjerds*);
  Nina's: 87 65 43 21 (*syvogfirs, femogtres, treogfyrre, enogtyve*).

  Danish words, not digits** — this is an audio course (e.g. *tolv, fireogtredive…*, never *12 34*;
  times already use words like *klokken otte*).
- **Translation-robust** — avoid constructions that gloss/translate awkwardly (written-out abbreviated
  addresses, lexical ambiguities).
- **Dialogue** — speakers address each other correctly (a clerk speaks *to* Maya, not in Maya's voice).
- **Scene-to-scene flow** — where natural, a scene may foreshadow the next or pay off the previous; don't force a bridge on every scene.
- **Translatable setting** — the real test is whether a place/thing **translates n-way**, not generic-vs-specific. Everyday places (a square, a park, a harbour, a museum) and **translatable references** (a known dish/statue/festival — *smørrebrød*, the Little Mermaid → *La Sirenita* etc.) are fine. **Opaque local place-names** (Nyhavn, Amalienborg) are NOT — they only transliterate. Keep any such reference to a **single deliberate anchor** per week. (Currency — *kroner* — is authentic **frame** like *Copenhagen*/*Nina*: kept and transliterated, not genericized — Maya lives in Denmark. - **Cast used sparingly** — the recurring cast (Nina, Peter, the family video call) appear only where a scene earns them, not every week; a week may stand on its own (Maya alone or with strangers).
- **The story never depicts Maya *learning* Danish** — she simply lives her life in Danish. Her growing fluency is shown, never stated as a milestone.

Canonical facts the **storyboard reviewer** checks a new week against. Updated as each week is
locked. The continuity lens treats everything here as established truth: a new week must not
*contradict* it, nor *re-introduce* (as if new) something already true.

## Maya (protagonist)
- From Mexico. A **software engineer** — she moved to Copenhagen in **January** because she landed
  a job at a software company here; the job is *why* she came. **31 when she arrived; turns 32 the
  following summer** (her birthday, wk26). Gradually settling in.
- First-person narrator throughout (her own voice).
- **Commute**: she takes the **bus** to work (wk6/7). She owns a **bicycle** but rides it mostly at
  weekends (wk7).
- **Weekly fixtures** (don't double-book): **gym Wednesday evenings** (wk7); **badminton Thursday evenings** (wk12); **volunteers Saturday mornings at a café** (wk20).

## Recurring cast
- **Nina** — Danish neighbour, met day 1 (week 1), Maya's first friend; lives in the same building. Kind, helpful.
- **Peter** — a colleague at Maya's software company; an easy, friendly workmate (met on her **first
  day, week 2**; recurs at the week-6 canteen lunch). Use him when a work colleague is needed rather
  than an anonymous *en kollega*.
- **Eva** — a **digital designer** on Maya's team; warm, creative (met **week 19** on the first big project). **Hosts Maya at her home in week 23.**
- **Family** — back home in Mexico, contact by video call: parents (*mor/far*), sister **Sofía**,
  brother **Diego**, and the family dog **Lola** (siblings + dog established in wk3's family call).

## Status ledger — what is TRUE by end of each week
### End of Week 1 (arrival)
- Maya lives in a **small TEMPORARY flat** (a place for the first weeks). She **already has an
  address** (this temp flat — she gave it to a taxi on arrival). It is *not* her permanent home yet
  ("a good start").
- She has **met Nina** (neighbour, first friend) — Nina lives **next door in the same building** as
  the temp flat (so Maya is already in Nina's building).
- She **has a job** — a software-engineering post at a software company; it is the reason she moved.
  She has **not started yet**: her first day at the office is in **week 2**.
- She does **NOT yet have**: a Danish phone number, a CPR number, an *official/registered* address.
- Foreshadowed (not yet true): her **own flat in week 4** — the temp flat is **already in Nina's
  building** (Nina is her neighbour from day 1), so week 4 is a *permanent* flat opening up
  in the **same building**: she leaves the temporary room for her own real home. CPR + phone + registration **and her first day at the software company** in **week 2**.

### End of A2 (≈ week 28)
- **Fully settled**: her own flat (wk4), a steady work routine, and the weekly fixtures (gym
  Wed / badminton Thu / café-volunteering Sat). She **cooks local dishes and hosts friends** now (wk22).
- Timeline: arrived January (deep winter) → **summer** by end of A2 → B1 moves into **autumn**.
- **Cast — all established, do NOT re-introduce as new:** Nina (+ her dog **Ludwig**, whom
  Maya dog-sat a weekend, wk24); Peter & **Eva** at work (Eva a digital designer, now a friend — she
  hosted Maya, wk23); **Kasper & Sara** from badminton (Maya cooked them dinner, wk22). Family video
  calls continue (mor/far, Sofía, Diego, dog Lola).

## Cross-cutting rules (every week)
- **Privacy** — the CPR number is sensitive (like an SSN). Never read it out / repeat it digit-by-digit;
  treat it as private, kept safe. Phone numbers MAY be shared/read aloud.
- **Fictional data** — any phone number etc. must be an obvious placeholder, never a plausibly-real
  number. Maya's phone: **12 34 56 78** (*tolv, fireogtredive, seksoghalvtreds, otteoghalvfjerds*);
  Nina's: 87 65 43 21 (*syvogfirs, femogtres, treogfyrre, enogtyve*).
- **Numbers woven into action** (ages, tickets, house numbers), not drilled. Don't use the SAME number
  for unrelated things in one scene (reads as if they're linked). A number **said aloud is written as
  Danish words, not digits** — this is an audio course (e.g. *tolv, fireogtredive…*, never *12 34*;
  times already use words like *klokken otte*).
- **Translation-robust** — avoid constructions that gloss/translate awkwardly (written-out abbreviated
  addresses, lexical ambiguities).
- **Dialogue** — speakers address each other correctly (a clerk speaks *to* Maya, not in Maya's voice).
- **Scene-to-scene flow** — where natural, a scene may foreshadow the next or pay off the previous; don't force a bridge on every scene.
- **Translatable setting** — the real test is whether a place/thing **translates n-way**, not generic-vs-specific. Everyday places (a square, a park, a harbour, a museum) and **translatable references** (a known dish/statue/festival — *smørrebrød*, the Little Mermaid → *La Sirenita* etc.) are fine. **Opaque local place-names** (Nyhavn, Amalienborg) are NOT — they only transliterate. Keep any such reference to a **single deliberate anchor** per week. (Currency — *kroner* — is authentic **frame** like *Copenhagen*/*Nina*: kept and transliterated, not genericized — Maya lives in Denmark. Spell amounts as words: Danish words only in the Danish (*femten kroner*), English in the storyboard and gloss (*fifteen kroner*).)
- **Cast used sparingly** — the recurring cast (Nina, Peter, the family video call) appear only where a scene earns them, not every week; a week may stand on its own (Maya alone or with strangers).
- **The story never depicts Maya *learning* Danish** — she simply lives her life in Danish. Her growing fluency is shown, never stated as a milestone.

## Maya (protagonist)
- From Mexico. A **software engineer** — she moved to Copenhagen in **January** because she landed
  a job at a software company here; the job is *why* she came. **31 when she arrived; turns 32 the
  following summer** (her birthday, wk26). Gradually settling in.
- First-person narrator throughout (her own voice).
- **Commute**: she takes the **bus** to work (wk6/7). She owns a **bicycle** but rides it mostly at
  weekends (wk7).
- **Weekly fixtures** (don't double-book): **gym Wednesday evenings** (wk7); **badminton Thursday evenings** (wk12); **volunteers Saturday mornings at a café** (wk20).

## Recurring cast
- **Nina** — Danish neighbour, met day 1 (week 1), Maya's first friend; lives in the same building. Kind, helpful.
- **Peter** — a colleague at Maya's software company; an easy, friendly workmate (met on her **first
  day, week 2**; recurs at the week-6 canteen lunch). Use him when a work colleague is needed rather
  than an anonymous *en kollega*.
- **Eva** — a **digital designer** on Maya's team; warm, creative (met **week 19** on the first big project). **Hosts Maya at her home in week 23.**
- **Family** — back home in Mexico, contact by video call: parents (*mor/far*), sister **Sofía**,

## Status ledger — what is TRUE by end of each week
### End of Week 1 (arrival)
- Maya lives in a **small TEMPORARY flat** (a place for the first weeks). She **already has an
  address** (this temp flat — she gave it to a taxi on arrival). It is *not* her permanent home yet

- She has **met Nina** (neighbour, first friend) — Nina lives **next door in the same building** as
  the temp flat (so Maya is already in Nina's building).
- She **has a job** — a software-engineering post at a software company; it is the reason she moved.
  She has **not started yet**: her first day at the office is in **week 2**.
- She does **NOT yet have**: a Danish phone number, a CPR number, an *official/registered* address.
- Foreshadowed (not yet true): her **own flat in week 4** — the temp flat is **already in Nina's
  building** (Nina is her neighbour from day 1), so week 4 is a *permanent* flat opening up
  in the **same building**: she leaves the temporary room for her own real home. CPR + phone + registration **and her first day at the software company** in **week 2**.

### End of A2 (≈ week 28)
- **Fully settled**: her own flat (wk4), a steady work routine, and the weekly fixtures (gym
  Wed / badminton Thu / café-volunteering Sat). She **cooks local dishes and hosts friends** now (wk22).
- Timeline: arrived January (deep winter) → **summer** by end of A2 → B1 moves into **autumn**.
- **Cast — all established, do NOT re-introduce as new:** Nina (+ her dog **Ludwig**, whom

## Cross-cutting rules (every week)
- **Privacy** — the CPR number is sensitive (like an SSN). Never read it out / repeat it digit-by-digit;
  treat it as private, kept safe. Phone numbers MAY be shared/read aloud.
- **Fictional data** — any phone number etc. must be an obvious placeholder, never a plausibly-real
  number. Maya's phone: **12 34 56 78** (*tolv, fireogtredive, seksoghalvtreds, otteoghalvfjerds*);
  Nina's: 87 65 43 21 (*syvogfirs, femogtres, treogfyrre, enogtyve*).
- **Numbers woven into action** (ages, tickets, house numbers), not drilled. Don't use the SAME number
  for unrelated things in one scene (reads as if they're linked). A number **said aloud is written as
  Danish words, not digits** — this is an audio course (e.g. *tolv, fireogtredive…*, never *12 34*;
  times already use words like *klokken otte*).
- **Translation-robust** — avoid constructions that gloss/translate awkwardly (written-out abbreviated
  addresses, lexical ambiguities).
- **Dialogue** — speakers address each other correctly (a clerk speaks *to* Maya, not in Maya's voice).
- **Scene-to-scene flow** — where natural, a scene may foreshadow the next or pay off the previous; don't force a bridge on every scene.
- **Translatable setting** — the real test is whether a place/thing **translates n-way**, not generic-vs-specific. Everyday places (a square, a park, a harbour, a museum) and **translatable references** (a known dish/statue/festival — *smørrebrød*, the Little Mermaid → *La Sirenita* etc.) are fine. **Opaque local place-names** (Nyhavn, Amalienborg) are NOT — they only transliterate. Keep any such reference to a **single deliberate anchor** per week. (Currency — *kroner* — is authentic **frame** like *Copenhagen*/*Nina*: kept and transliterated, not genericized — Maya lives in Denmark. Spell amounts as words: Danish words only in the Danish (*femten kroner*), English in the storyboard and gloss (*fifteen kroner*).)
- **Cast used sparingly** — the recurring cast (Nina, Peter, the family video call) appear only where a scene earns them, not every week; a week may stand on its own (Maya alone or with strangers).
- **The story never depicts Maya *learning* Danish** — she simply lives her life in Danish. Her growing fluency is shown, never stated as a milestone.

- **Scene-to-scene flow** — where natural, a scene may foreshadow the next or pay off the previous; don't force a bridge on every scene.
- **Translatable setting** — the real test is whether a place/thing **translates n-way**, not generic-vs-specific. Everyday places (a square, a park, a harbour, a museum) and **translatable references** (a known dish/statue/festival — *smørrebrød*, the Little Mermaid → *La Sirenita* etc.) are fine. **Opaque local place-names** (Nyhavn, Amalienborg) are NOT — they only transliterate. # Story Bible — Maya's first year (continuity ground-truth)

Canonical facts the **storyboard reviewer** checks a new week against. Updated as each week is
locked. The continuity lens treats everything here as established truth: a new week must not
*contradict* it, nor *re-introduce* (as if new) something already true.

## Maya (protagonist)
- From Mexico. A **software engineer** — she moved to Copenhagen in **January** because she landed
  a job at a software company here; the job is *why* she came. **31 when she arrived; turns 32 the
  following summer** (her birthday, wk26). Gradually settling in.
- First-person narrator throughout (her own voice).
- **Commute**: she takes the **bus** to work (wk6/7). She owns a **bicycle** but rides it mostly at
  weekends (wk7).
- **Weekly fixtures** (don't double-book): **gym Wednesday evenings** (wk7); **badminton Thursday evenings** (wk12); **volunteers Saturday mornings at a café** (wk20).

## Recurring cast
- **Nina** — Danish neighbour, met day 1 (week 1), Maya's first friend; lives in the same building. Kind, helpful.
- **Peter** — a colleague at Maya's software company; an easy, friendly workmate (met on her **first
  day, week 2**; recurs at the week-6 canteen lunch). Use him when a work colleague is needed rather
  than an anonymous *en kollega*.
- **Eva** — a **digital designer** on Maya's team; warm, creative (met **week 19** on the first big project). **Hosts Maya at her home in week 23.**
- **Family** — back home in Mexico, contact by video call: parents (*mor/far*), sister **Sofía**,
  brother **Diego**, and the family dog **Lola** (siblings + dog established in wk3's family call).

## Status ledger — what is TRUE by end of each week
### End of Week 1 (arrival)
- Maya lives in a **small TEMPORARY flat** (a place for the first weeks). She **already has an
  address** (this temp flat — she gave it to a taxi on arrival). It is *not* her permanent home yet
  ("a good start").
- She has **met Nina** (neighbour, first friend) — Nina lives **next door in the same building** as
  the temp flat (so Maya is already in Nina's building).
- She **has a job** — a software-engineering post at a software company; it is the reason she moved.
  She has **not started yet**: her first day at the office is in **week 2**.
- She does **NOT yet have**: a Danish phone number, a CPR number, an *official/registered* address.
- Foreshadowed (not yet true): her **own flat in week 4** — the temp flat is **already in Nina's
  building** (Nina is her neighbour from day 1), so week 4 is a *permanent* flat opening up
  in the **same building**: she leaves the temporary room for her own real home. CPR + phone + registration **and her first day at the software company** in **week 2**.

### End of A2 (≈ week 28)
- **Fully settled**: her own flat (wk4), a steady work routine, and the weekly fixtures (gym
  Wed / badminton Thu / café-volunteering Sat). She **cooks local dishes and hosts friends** now (wk22).
- Timeline: arrived January (deep winter) → **summer** by end of A2 → B1 moves into **autumn**.
- **Cast — all established, do NOT re-introduce as new:** Nina (+ her dog **Ludwig**, whom
  Maya dog-sat a weekend, wk24); Peter & **Eva** at work (Eva a digital designer, now a friend — she
  hosted Maya, wk23); **Kasper & Sara** from badminton (Maya cooked them dinner, wk22). Family video
  calls continue (mor/far, Sofía, Diego, dog Lola).

## Cross-cutting rules (every week)
- **Privacy** — the CPR number is sensitive (like an SSN). Never read it out / repeat it digit-by-digit;
  treat it as private, kept safe. Phone numbers MAY be shared/read aloud.
- **Fictional data** — any phone number etc. must be an obvious placeholder, never a plausibly-real
  number. Maya's phone: **12 34 56 78** (*tolv, fireogtredive, seksoghalvtreds, otteoghalvfjerds*);
  Nina's: 87 65 43 21 (*syvogfirs, femogtres, treogfyrre, enogtyve*).
- **Numbers woven into action** (ages, tickets, house numbers), not drilled. Don't use the SAME number
  for unrelated things in one scene (reads as if they're linked). A number **said aloud is written as
  Danish words, not digits** — this is an audio course (e.g. *tolv, fireogtredive…*, never *12 34*;
  times already use words like *klokken otte*).
- **Translation-robust** — avoid constructions that gloss/translate awkwardly (written-out abbreviated
  addresses, lexical ambiguities).
- **Dialogue** — speakers address each other correctly (a clerk speaks *to* Maya, not in Maya's voice).
- **Scene-to-scene flow** — where natural, a scene may foreshadow the next or pay off the previous; don't force a bridge on every scene.
- **Translatable setting** — the real test is whether a place/thing **translates n-way**, not generic-vs-specific. Everyday places (a square, a park, a harbour, a museum) and **translatable references** (a known dish/statue/festival — *smørrebrød*, the Little Mermaid → *La Sirenita* etc.) are fine. **Opaque local place-names** (Nyhavn, Amalienborg) are NOT — they only transliterate. Keep any such reference to a **single deliberate anchor** per week. (Currency — *kroner* — is authentic **frame** like *Copenhagen*/*Nina*: kept and transliterated, not genericized — Maya lives in Denmark. Spell amounts as words: Danish words only in the Danish (*femten kroner*), English in the storyboard and gloss (*fifteen kroner*).)
- **Cast used sparingly** — the recurring cast (Nina, Peter, the family video call) appear only where a scene earns them, not every week; a week may stand on its own (Maya alone or with strangers).
- **The story never depicts Maya *learning* Danish** — she simply lives her life in Danish. Her growing fluency is shown, never stated as a milestone.

- Foreshadowed (not yet true): her **own flat in week 4** — the temp flat is **already in Nina's
  building** (Nina is her neighbour from day 1), so week 4 is a *permanent* flat opening up
  in the **same building**: she leaves the temporary room for her own real home. CPR + phone + registration **and her first day at the software company** in **week 2**.

### End of A2 (≈ week 28)
- **Fully settled**: her own flat (wk4), a steady work routine, and the weekly fixtures (gym
  Wed / badminton Thu / café-volunteering Sat). She **cooks local dishes and hosts friends** now (wk22).
- Timeline: arrived January (deep winter) → **summer** by end of A2 → B1 moves into **autumn**.
- **Cast — all established, do NOT re-introduce as new:** Nina (+ her dog **Ludwig**, whom
  Maya dog-sat a weekend, wk24); Peter & **Eva** at work (Eva a digital designer, now a friend — she
  hosted Maya, wk23); **Kasper & Sara** from badminton (Maya cooked them dinner, wk22). Family video
  calls continue (mor/far, Sofía, Diego, dog Lola).

## Cross-cutting rules (every week)
- **Privacy** — the CPR number is sensitive (like an SSN). Never read it out / repeat it digit-by-digit;
  treat it as private, kept safe. Phone numbers MAY be shared/read aloud.
- **Fictional data** — any phone number etc. must be an obvious placeholder, never a plausibly-real
  number. Maya's phone: **12 34 56 78** (*tolv, fireogtredive, seksoghalvtreds, otteoghalvfjerds*);
  Nina's: 87 65 43 21 (*syvogfirs, femogtres, treogfyrre, enogtyve*).
- **Numbers woven into action** (ages, tickets, house numbers), not drilled. Don't use the SAME number
  for unrelated things in one scene (reads as if they're linked). A number **said aloud is written as
  Danish words, not digits** — this is an audio course (e.g. *tolv, fireogtredive…*, never *12 34*;
  times already use words like *klokken otte*).
- **Translation-robust** — avoid constructions that gloss/translate awkwardly (written-out abbreviated
  addresses, lexical ambiguities).
- **Dialogue** — speakers address each other correctly (a clerk speaks *to* Maya, not in Maya's voice).
- **Scene-to-scene flow** — where natural, a scene may foreshadow the next or pay off the previous; don't force a bridge on every scene.
- **Translatable setting** — the real test is whether a place/thing **translates n-way**, not generic-vs-specific. Everyday places (a square, a park, a harbour, a museum) and **translatable references** (a known dish/statue/festival — *smørrebrød*, the Little Mermaid → *La Sirenita* etc.) are fine. **Opaque local place-names** (Nyhavn, Amalienborg) are NOT — they only transliterate. Keep any such reference to a **single deliberate anchor** per week. (Currency — *kroner* — is authentic **frame** like *Copenhagen*/*Nina*: kept and transliterated, not genericized — Maya lives in Denmark. Spell amounts as words: Danish words only in the Danish (*femten kroner*), English in the storyboard and gloss (*fifteen kroner*).)
- **Cast used sparingly** — the recurring cast (Nina, Peter, the family video call) appear only where a scene earns them, not every week; a week may stand on its own (Maya alone or with strangers).
- **The story never depicts Maya *learning* Danish** — she simply lives her life in Danish. Her growing fluency is shown, never stated as a milestone.

--- end bible ---
Use the bible to tell a real CONTRADICTION from a LEGITIMATE change the story intends (Maya moves from
a temporary flat to her own flat; her job is not-yet-started then started; winter deepens). A narrated
transition is NOT a contradiction.

# Story Bible — Maya's first year (continuity ground-truth)

Canonical facts the **storyboard reviewer** checks a new week against. Updated as each week is
locked. The continuity lens treats everything here as established truth: a new week must not
*contradict* it, nor *re-introduce* (as if new) something already true.

## Maya (protagonist)
- From Mexico. A **software engineer** — she moved to Copenhagen in **January** because she landed
  a job at a software company here; the job is *why* she came. **31 when she arrived; turns 32 the
  following summer** (her birthday, wk26). Gradually settling in.
- First-person narrator throughout (her own voice).
- **Commute**: she takes the **bus** to work (wk6/7). She owns a **bicycle** but rides it mostly at
  weekends (wk7).
- **Weekly fixtures** (don't double-book): **gym Wednesday evenings** (wk7); **badminton Thursday evenings** (wk12); **volunteers Saturday mornings at a café** (wk20).

## Recurring cast
- **Nina** — Danish neighbour, met day 1 (week 1), Maya's first friend; lives in the same building. Kind, helpful.
- **Peter** — a colleague at Maya's software company; an easy, friendly workmate (met on her **first
  day, week 2**; recurs at the week-6 canteen lunch). Use him when a work colleague is needed rather

- **Eva** — a **digital designer** on Maya's team; warm, creative (met **week 19** on the first big project). **Hosts Maya at her home in week 23.**

## Status ledger — what is TRUE by end of each week
### End of Week 1 (arrival)
- Maya lives in a **small TEMPORARY flat** (a place for the first weeks). She **already has an
  address** (this temp flat — she gave it to a taxi on arrival). It is *not* her permanent home yet
  ("a good start").
- She has **met Nina** (neighbour, first friend) — Nina lives **next door in the same building** as
  the temp flat (so Maya is already in Nina's building).
- She **has a job** — a software-engineering post at a software company; it is the reason she moved.
  She has **not started yet**: her first day at the office is in **week 2**.
- She does **NOT yet have**: a Danish phone number, a CPR number, an *official/registered* address.
- Foreshadowed (not yet true): her **own flat in week 4** — the temp flat is **already in Nina's
  building** (Nina is her neighbour from day 1), so week 4 is a *permanent* flat opening up
  in the **same building**: she leaves the temporary room for her own real home. CPR + phone + registration **and her first day at the software company** in **week 2**.

### End of A2 (≈ week 28)

  Wed / badminton Thu / café-volunteering Sat). She **cooks local dishes and hosts friends** now (wk22).

- **Privacy** — the CPR number is sensitive (like an SSN). Never read it out / repeat it digit-by-digit;

  times already use words like *klokken otte*).
- **Translation-robust** — avoid constructions that gloss/translate awkwardly (written-out abbreviated
  addresses, lexical ambiguities).
- **Dialogue** — speakers address each other correctly (a clerk speaks *to* Maya, not in Maya's voice).
- **Scene-to-scene flow** — where natural, a scene may foreshadow the next or pay off the previous; don't force a bridge on every scene.
- **Translatable setting** — the real test is whether a place/thing **translates n-way**, not generic-vs-specific. Everyday places (a square, a park, a harbour, a museum) and **translatable references** (a known dish/statue/festival — *smørrebrød*, the Little Mermaid → *La Sirenita* etc.) are fine. **Opaque local place-names** (Nyhavn, Amalienborg) are NOT — they only transliterate. - **The story never depicts Maya *learning* Danish** — she simply lives her life in Danish. Her growing fluency is shown, never stated as a milestone.

# Story Bible — Maya's first year (continuity ground-truth)

## Maya (protagonist)

  following summer** (her birthday, wk26). Gradually settling in.

### End of Week 1 (arrival)

  address** (this temp flat — she gave it to a taxi on arrival). It is *not* her permanent home yet
  ("a good start").

  She has **not started yet**: her first day at the office is in **week 2**.
- She does **NOT yet have**: a Danish phone number, a CPR number, an *official/registered* address.

  in the **same building**: she leaves the temporary room for her own real home. CPR + phone + registration **and her first day at the software company** in **week 2**.

### End of A2 (≈ week 28)

  times already use words like *klokken otte*).
- **Translation-robust** — avoid constructions that gloss/translate awkwardly (written-out abbreviated
  addresses, lexical ambiguities).

- **Scene-to-scene flow** — where natural, a scene may foreshadow the next or pay off the previous; don't force a bridge on every scene.
- **Translatable setting** — the real test is whether a place/thing **translates n-way**, not generic-vs-specific. Everyday places (a square, a park, a harbour, a museum) and **translatable references** (a known dish/statue/festival — *smørrebrød*, the Little Mermaid → *La Sirenita* etc.) are fine. **Opaque local place-names** (Nyhavn, Amalienborg) are NOT — they only transliterate. - **The story never depicts Maya *learning* Danish** — she simply lives her life in Danish. Her growing fluency is shown, never stated as a milestone.
